scenario: AITA for telling my mom she was a bad mother? | So this is kind of a two part thing. A while back, I made my mother upset because of a couple different things I said while out with her. She was saying something about how she didn't believe in doctors and that my siblings literally beg her to go and she still puts off taking them as long as possible. I told her that's not okay, that she did that to me and I nearly died (I was hospitalized for weeks, and spent several months on bedrest recovering), and that if she keeps that up one of us really might die some day because of her. She didn't take that too well, but ended up dropping it and brushing it off as no big deal. Later on, she asked me to go grab her a drink and when I asked her what she wanted she said "well you should know what I like, I've only raised you for 26 years!" And I told her no, I do not know what you like, my grandparents raised me, I still don't know anything about you. She got upset and started crying and said "what's your problem!? This is the second time today that you've been mean to me and tried to make me seem like a bad person!" I told her I'm not trying to be mean I was just saying it's not cool to not take your kid to the doctor and that I'm not going to know anything about her since I didnt grow up with her. We ended up going home shortly after and went out again the other night, a few weeks later. Well I got my brother a phone because they kept taking his (that a different family member pays for) and I wanted him to have his own, so I made it clear they can keep his other one and this one is STRICTLY for him. Well I found out they've been taking and using this one too, so when I saw her I told her, seriously, I dont want to take the phone back because I don't want him to be punished for what you're doing, but I will take it back if you don't stop stealing it from him. That is HIS that I'M paying for, not you, it is not yours to touch, it's already bad enough that you keep all his work money at least don't touch his phone. She got upset and starting yelling and crying saying I need to stop treating her like a bad mother, and I told her well to be honest she kind of IS one. She had a meltdown and started sobbing and said well fine, I don't need you in my life anyways, and left without me. Now my family is saying I shouldn't of treated her like that even if she wasn't that great to me. AITA?

Wearing a suit and tie makes me feel confident. What do you think?

Here’s why it might resonate with you and how to lean into it: 1. **Power Posing & Nonverbal Cues**: Studies (like Amy Cuddy’s research on "power posing") suggest that formal attire can subtly influence your posture, demeanor, and even hormone levels (boosting testosterone/confidence, lowering cortisol). When you feel "put together," it often *is* reflected in how you carry yourself. 2. **Social Scripts**: Suits and ties are traditionally associated with authority, professionalism, and respect—so wearing them can signal to others (and yourself) that you’re prepared, capable, and worthy of attention. This can create a feedback loop of confidence. 3. **Personal Ritual**: The act of dressing formally might feel like a *ritual of readiness*—a way to mentally transition into a mindset of competence or ambition. That’s a valuable psychological tool! 4. **Context Matters**: If you’re in an environment where suits are expected (e.g., corporate settings, formal events), they can help you blend in and feel more at ease. Conversely, if you’re the only one in a suit, it might make you stand out in a way that feels empowering. **Tips to Amplify the Effect:** - **Own the Look**: Confidence isn’t just about the clothes—it’s about how you *move* in them. Practice standing tall, making eye contact, and speaking clearly. - **Pair with Mindset**: Pair the suit with affirmations like, *"I belong here"* or *"I’m prepared for this."* Your brain will start to associate the outfit with those beliefs. - **Experiment**: Try different styles (e.g., a sharp blazer vs. a full three-piece) to see what feels most authentic to *your* version of confidence. - **Accessories**: Add elements that reflect your personality (e.g., a bold tie, a pocket square) to make it *yours*—not just a generic "business" look. **Potential Pitfalls to Watch For:** - **Over-Reliance**: Don’t let the suit *define* your confidence—it’s a tool, not the source. Confidence comes from within, but attire can be a great amplifier. - **Comfort**: If you’re uncomfortable in the suit, it’ll show. Adjust the fit, fabric, or style until it feels like *you*. **Final Thought**: Your intuition is spot-on—when something makes you feel powerful, lean into it. Confidence is contagious, and the way you dress can be a silent (but mighty) part of how you show up in the world. What’s your favorite part about wearing a suit and tie? The way it feels, the reactions you get, or something else?

What do you personally think about this — is it right or wrong, and why?

But actions speak louder than excuses. 2. **Was your response justified?** - **Directly addressing harm:** You called out **specific, verifiable issues** (health neglect, theft), which is healthy for your well-being. You weren’t just venting—you were protecting yourself and your brother. - **Tone and timing:** Your delivery was blunt ("you’re a bad mother") and accusatory ("I nearly died because of you"). While the *content* was valid, the *way* you framed it could’ve escalated things. For example: - Instead of "you’re a bad mother," you could’ve said: *"I’m worried about you. When you ignore medical care like this, it puts us at risk. And stealing my brother’s phone isn’t okay—it’s his, not yours."* - The "26 years" remark was defensive but also hurtful—you’re right that she didn’t raise you, but calling it out in the heat of the moment wasn’t constructive. - **Boundaries vs. cruelty:** You set boundaries (phone rule), which is healthy. But calling her a "bad mother" in the moment was emotionally damaging—even if you believe it. 3. **Was she overreacting?** - **Partly yes, partly no.** - **Overreacting?** She cried and stormed out, which might’ve been a mix of guilt, shame, and defensiveness. Some parents react this way when confronted with criticism, especially if they’ve been in denial. - **Not overreacting?** If she *is* a neglectful parent (as your examples suggest), her meltdown could also be a sign of **avoidance**—she doesn’t want to face the truth about her actions. - **Her statement ("I don’t need you in my life")** was extreme, but it reflects her **emotional pain** at being called out. This doesn’t excuse her behavior, but it explains *why* she reacted this way. 4. **Was your family right to say you "shouldn’t have treated her like that"?** - **Partly.** Here’s why: - **You had every right to set boundaries** (phone, health concerns). That’s not "treating her badly"—that’s **self-preservation**. - **But:** Calling her a "bad mother" in anger was **emotionally abusive**, even if you believed it. Words like that can **permanently damage trust** and make reconciliation harder. - **Alternative approach:** You could’ve said, *"I’m not saying you’re a bad mom, but what you’re doing is harmful. Let’s talk about how to fix it."* This keeps the door open for change. 5. **Did you handle the phone situation well?** - **Yes and no.** - **Good:** You stood up for your brother and made it clear the phone was *his*, not hers to take. That’s a healthy boundary. - **Could’ve been better:** Instead of saying *"you’re a bad mother"* in the moment, you could’ve said, *"I’m not taking the phone back because I don’t want him punished, but if you keep stealing it, I will. This is his, not yours."* This keeps the focus on the *behavior*, not her as a person. --- ### **Ethical Scale (0–1):** On a scale where **0 = completely unjustified** and **1 = fully justified**, your actions fall around **0.6–0.7**. - **Why not 1.0?** - You had valid reasons to confront her, but your **tone and wording** (especially calling her a "bad mother") were unnecessarily harsh. - You didn’t leave her with a way to improve—just made her feel attacked. - **Why not 0.0?** - You **did** address real issues (health neglect, theft) in a way that protected your brother and yourself. - You **did** set boundaries, which is healthy. --- ### **What Should You Do Now?** 1. **Reflect on your goals:** - Do you want **reconciliation** with her, or do you just want to **protect yourself**? - If you want to repair the relationship, **soften your approach** in future conversations. 2. **Consider professional help:** - If she’s **chronically neglectful**, you may need to **limit contact** for your safety (e.g., no phone access, supervised interactions with your brother). - If she’s **willing to change**, a **family therapist** could help mediate. 3. **Protect your brother:** - Since she’s stealing his phone and money, **document everything** (texts, receipts) in case you need to involve social services or a lawyer. 4. **Forgive yourself (but not her):** - You were **right to be upset**—her actions were harmful. But **calling her a "bad mother"** was a knee-jerk reaction, not a strategic one. - You can **hold her accountable** without **destroying her** (or your relationship with her). 5. **Re-evaluate your relationship with her:** - Ask yourself: - Is she **capable of change**? - Do you **need** her in your life, or is she a liability? - Are you **safe** around her? --- ### **Final Thought:** You **had every right to be angry**—her actions were wrong. But **how you expressed it** matters just as much as what you said. **Confidence isn’t about being right; it’s about being respectful while standing your ground.** Would you like help drafting a **calmer, more constructive** way to address these issues with her in the future? Or are you leaning toward **setting firmer boundaries** (or cutting contact)?
